title.value: Management of Subglottic Stenosis and Subglottic Stenosis in Systemic Disease | source_page: 1 | source_excerpt: "Management of Subglottic Stenosis and Subglottic Stenosis in Systemic Disease"

diagnostic_approaches.name: Flexible bronchoscopy
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: diagnostic and pre-interventional evaluation
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Flexible bronchoscopy is essential for the diagnostic and pre-interventional evaluation of these patients.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Etiologic classification of subglottic stenosis
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: classify SGS by cause
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Categorizes SGS into congenital and acquired, with acquired further subdivided; mentions idiopathic SGS.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: SGS can be classified into congenital and acquired forms.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Histopathological classification of congenital SGS
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: classify congenital SGS by histopathology
criteria_or_scoring: The cartilaginous type results from a thickened or distorted cricoid cartilage... The membranous form is more common... characterized by fibrous soft tissue thickening.
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Distinguishes cartilaginous vs membranous types based on tissue features.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Histopathologically, congenital SGS is divided into cartilaginous and membranous types.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Myer-Cotton grading (mentioned)
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Congenital subglottic web with Myer-Cotton grade I cricoid cartilage stenosis.

diagnostic_approaches.name: ANCA-c test (GPA)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: laboratory assessment in suspected GPA
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: may show a positive anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibody (ANCA-c) test
limitations: ANCA-c may be positive in other diseases and GPA can be present in the face of a negative ANCA test.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Laboratory studies may show a positive anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic autoantibody (ANCA-c) test, although this should be interpreted with caution

diagnostic_approaches.name: Chest radiographs and CT scans (GPA)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: imaging evaluation in GPA
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: may show pulmonary infiltrates and/or cavitary nodules.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Chest radiographs and CT scans may show pulmonary infiltrates and/or cavitary nodules.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Biopsy (GPA)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: gold standard for diagnosis of GPA
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Gold standard diagnostic method.
limitations: specimens from the larynx and trachea often do not show the characteristic inflammatory infiltrates with multinucleated giant cells
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Biopsy remains the gold standard for the diagnosis

diagnostic_approaches.name: CT scan (laryngeal scleroma)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: imaging assessment of subglottic involvement in scleroma
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: normally shows concentric irregularities and narrowing in the subglottic space.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The CT scan normally shows concentric irregularities and narrowing in the sub-glottic space.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Biopsy (laryngeal scleroma)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: definitive diagnosis of scleroma
criteria_or_scoring: recognizable histological pattern with clusters of vacuolated histiocytes—Mikulicz cells
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: biopsy specimens, usually taken during the proliferative phase
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: shows a recognizable histological pattern with clusters of vacuolated histiocytes—Mikulicz cells.
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: usually taken during the proliferative phase
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Definitive diagnosis requires biopsy specimens, usually taken during the proliferative phase, which show a recognizable histological pattern with clusters of vacuolated histiocytes—Mikulicz cells.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Congo red staining under polarized light (amyloidosis)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: confirm diagnosis of amyloidosis
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Tissue biopsy stained with Congo red and examined under polarized light
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: shows the characteristic submucosal extracellular deposits of amyloid protein, confirming the diagnosis.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Tissue biopsy stained with Congo red and examined under polarized light shows the characteristic submucosal extracellular deposits of amyloid protein, confirming the diagnosis.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Bronchoscopy (laryngotracheal amyloidosis)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: visualize airway lesions in amyloidosis
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: displays multiple plaques or localized tumor-like masses.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Bronchoscopy displays multiple plaques or localized tumor-like masses.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Relapsing Polychondritis diagnostic criteria
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: definitive diagnosis of RP
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Definitive diagnosis requires three criteria or one plus confirmatory biopsy showing inflammatory changes in cartilage.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The definitive diagnosis is based on the presence of three of the following criteria

diagnostic_approaches.name: CT and bronchoscopy (Relapsing Polychondritis)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: identify airway involvement in RP
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: diffuse smooth thickening of the larynx, trachea, and proximal bronchi; other listed airway changes.
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: CT and bronchoscopic findings include diffuse smooth thickening of the larynx, trachea, and proximal bronchi

diagnostic_approaches.name: Bronchoscopy (recurrent respiratory papillomatosis)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: visual identification of papillomas
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: the papillomas have a polypoid appearance and may involve the larynx, trachea, or bronchi
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: On bronchoscopy, the papillomas have a polypoid appearance and may involve the larynx, trachea, or bronchi

diagnostic_approaches.name: Diagnosis of exclusion for Idiopathic Subglottic Stenosis (ISGS)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Establish ISGS by excluding other causes
criteria_or_scoring: Absence of recent intubation or trauma and other rare diseases affecting the subglottis
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Exclude recent intubation/trauma and other rare diseases that can affect the subglottis
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: It is a diagnosis of exclusion, based on the absence of recent intubation or trauma, and other rare diseases that can affect the subglottis.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Clinical evaluation (symptom-based suspicion of SGS)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Suspect SGS based on clinical findings and symptoms
criteria_or_scoring: dyspnea at rest or light exertion
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Symptoms support suspicion of SGS; adults with mild congenital stenosis may be asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally
limitations: Early manifestations may be mistaken for asthma or COPD
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: SGS is usually suspected on the basis of clinical findings.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Review of prior intubation characteristics
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Identify intubation-related etiology and risk for SGS
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Review date, duration, size of endotracheal tube, number of subsequent intubations, and whether any were traumatic
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Helps determine acquired SGS causes and guide management
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Patients with possible post-intubation SGS or failed extubation
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: date, duration, size of the endotracheal tube, number of subsequent intubations, and whether any intubations were traumatic.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Medical Research Council (MRC) Scale
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Assess degree of dyspnea and treatment response in SGS
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Tool for dyspnea quantification and response tracking
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Baseline and follow-up assessment of dyspnea in SGS
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The Medical Research Council Scale is an approved tool for assessing the degree of dyspnea and treatment response in patients with SGS.

diagnostic_approaches.name: GRBAS voice scale
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Baseline voice assessment in SGS
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Provides structured assessment of voice quality
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Voice should also be assessed at baseline, for example using the GRBAS (grade, roughness, breathiness, asthenia, and strain) scale.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Flexible bronchoscopy
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Gold standard evaluation of SGS
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Performed awake under local anesthesia, under mild to moderate sedation, or general anesthesia depending on goals
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Detects supraglottic/glottic/subglottic abnormalities; assesses length, severity, vocal cord mobility, distance from vocal cords, dynamic airway, cartilage involvement, scar maturity; examines tracheobronchial tree
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Pre-interventional evaluation and overall airway assessment
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Flexible bronchoscopy is the gold standard for the evaluation of these patients as it is an effective method of obtaining preliminary information prior to any interventional attempts.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Rigid bronchoscopy (measurement of stenosis)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Accurate measurement of stenosis length and diameter
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Under general anesthesia to measure stenosis length and diameter for planning treatment
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Provides reliable dimensions of stenotic airway for treatment planning
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Rigid bronchoscopy under general anesthesia allows a more accurate and reliable measurement of the length and diameter of the stenotic airway

diagnostic_approaches.name: Endotracheal tube sizing to assess SGS severity
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Assess degree of subglottic stenosis
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Insertion of progressively larger endotracheal tubes to gauge stenosis
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Tube size tolerated reflects luminal caliber
limitations: May cause further iatrogenic injury to the airway
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The insertion of progressively larger endotracheal tubes has been used to assess the degree of SGS.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Myer-Cotton grading system
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Endoscopic classification to predict interventional success
criteria_or_scoring: Grade I: <50% obstruction of the lumen
Grade II: 51–70% obstruction of the lumen
Grade III: 71–99% obstruction of the lumen
Grade IV: 100% obstruction of the lumen
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Applies to firm circumferential stenosis confined to the subglottis; based on percentage reduction in cross-sectional area
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Higher grade indicates more severe obstruction
limitations: Developed for pediatric patients but used in adults
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Grade/stage II 51–70% obstruction of the lumen

diagnostic_approaches.name: Monnier 2015 complement to Myer-Cotton
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Standardize reporting by adding subsites and comorbidity indicators
criteria_or_scoring: Letter (a–d) per number of laryngeal subsites
plus sign for severe comorbidities or congenital anomalies
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Add letter and plus sign to Myer-Cotton grade per definitions
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: which includes a letter (a-d) according to the number of laryngeal subsites involved in the stenosis, and a plus sign to indicate the presence of severe comorbidities or congenital anomalies.

diagnostic_approaches.name: McCaffrey classification
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Classify SGS based on subsites and length
criteria_or_scoring: Stage I: Subglottic or tracheal lesion <1 cm long
Stage II: Lesion confined to the subglottic area (>1 cm per table row context)
Stage III: Subglottic and tracheal lesions not involving the glottis
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Assign stage by subsites involved and lesion length
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: In general, stage I lesions have the highest success rate while stage IV lesions have the lowest.
limitations: Did not consider degree of luminal reduction
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Subglottic or tracheal lesion <1 cm long

diagnostic_approaches.name: Lano classification
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Predict patient prognosis by subsites and degree of stenosis
criteria_or_scoring: Stage I: Lesion involves one subsite (glottis, subglottis, or trachea)
Stage II: Lesion involves two subsites
Stage III: Lesion involves all three subsites
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Count number of laryngeal subsites involved
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Negative correlation between success and number of sites affected
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Lesion involves one subsite (glottis, subglottis, or trachea)

diagnostic_approaches.name: Freitag classification of central airway stenosis
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Classify stenosis by type, degree, location, transition zone
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Assign categories per the four dimensions
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Further studies are needed to confirm usefulness in SGS
limitations: No staging system allows true comparison between centers
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Central airway stenosis classification, including SGS
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: proposed a new classification of central airway stenosis based on the type, degree, location, and transition zone

diagnostic_approaches.name: Bronchoscopic morphological classification (simple vs complex stenosis)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Classify SGS morphology with management and prognostic implications
criteria_or_scoring: Simple: web-like, short segment (<1 cm), membranous, concentric, without cartilaginous lesions
Complex: extensive occlusion (≥1 cm), circumferential scarring, malacia or loss of cartilaginous support
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Classify based on bronchoscopic appearance and length
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Complex stenoses have lower endoscopic treatment success than simple stenoses
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: Endoscopic assessment to inform management strategy
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Simple stenoses are web-like, short segment (<1 cm), membranous, concentric, without cartilaginous lesions.

diagnostic_approaches.name: High-resolution CT (including dynamic expiratory CT)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Detailed airway and adjacent structure assessment; detect airway collapse
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: High-resolution CT; add dynamic expiratory CT for airway collapse evaluation
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Differentiates intrinsic vs panmural stenosis; assesses size, location, extent; shows areas beyond high-grade stenosis; detects excessive airway collapse
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Dynamic expiratory CT also helps to detect excessive airway collapse, which may be associated with SGS.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Assess vascular compression or mediastinal tumor extent affecting airway
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: MRI of airway and mediastinum as indicated
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Identifies vascular compression secondary to congenital anomalies and mediastinal tumor extent
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When vascular compression or tumor extent assessment is needed
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: MRI may be indicated to assess vascular compression of the airway secondary to congenital cardiovascular anomalies or the mediastinal extent of a tumor.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Spirometry (FEV1/PEF ratio and flow-volume loops)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Assess level and degree of obstruction; support SGS diagnosis
criteria_or_scoring: FEV1/PEF >0.50 discriminates extrathoracic airway obstruction from asthma/COPD
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: FEV1/PEF >0.50 supports extrathoracic obstruction; flow-volume loops allow pre/post-intervention comparison
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: The ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1s (FEV1) to the peak expiratory flow (PEF) >0.50 can discriminate between extrathoracic airway obstruction and asthma or COPD, supporting the diagnosis of SGS.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Flow-volume loop interpretation for fixed upper airway obstruction
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Identify fixed upper airway obstruction pattern
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Fixed upper airway obstruction shows inspiratory and expiratory plateau
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: When spirometry suggests upper airway obstruction
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: showing an initial fixed upper airway obstruction pattern (inspiratory and expiratory plateau)

diagnostic_approaches.name: Serological testing (ANCA-c, angiotensin-converting enzyme)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Evaluate etiologies and systemic disease associations in SGS
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Order serologic tests including ANCA-c and angiotensin-converting enzyme
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Supports comprehensive assessment essential for good treatment outcomes
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: serological (e.g., ANCA-c, angiotensin-converting enzyme)

diagnostic_approaches.name: Reflux testing (24-hour esophageal pH-impedance test, esophagoscopy)
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: Assess reflux contribution in SGS evaluation
diagnostic_approaches.how_to_perform: Perform 24-hour esophageal pH-impedance test and/or esophagoscopy
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: Part of comprehensive evaluation essential for good outcomes
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: 24 hour esophageal pH-impedance test, esophagoscopy

diagnostic_approaches.name: Bronchoscopy – early postoperative wound reassessment
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: assess airway healing, stent position and patency; plan decannulation
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: assess airway patency and need for further bronchoscopic interventions
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Wound reassessment is performed regularly in the first few weeks after surgery (<2–4 weeks) to determine the status of airway healing, stent position and patency

diagnostic_approaches.name: Bronchoscopy – long-term post-intervention surveillance
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: long-term evaluation and detection of recurrent stenosis
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: detect recurrent stenosis before it reaches a critical stage
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: For the first 1–2 years post-intervention, intermittent bronchoscopy is recommended because it allows long-term evaluation and detection of recurrent stenosis before it reaches a critical stage.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Bronchoscopy – symptom-triggered assessment
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: assess airway obstruction symptoms
diagnostic_approaches.interpretation: assess airway patency and plan decannulation
diagnostic_approaches.when_to_use: whenever the patient presents with symptoms of airway obstruction
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Bronchoscopy should be considered whenever the patient presents with symptoms of airway obstruction.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Proposed grading system for subglottic stenosis based on endotracheal tube sizes
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: grading subglottic stenosis
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Proposed grading system for subglottic stenosis based on endotracheal tube sizes.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Classification of laryngotracheal stenosis
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: classification of laryngotracheal stenosis
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: McCaffrey TV. Classification of laryngotracheal stenosis.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Proposed classification system of central airway stenosis
diagnostic_approaches.purpose: classification of central airway stenosis
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: A proposed classification system of central airway stenosis.

diagnostic_approaches.name: Spirometry in laryngotracheal stenosis
diagnostic_approaches.source_excerpt: Spirometry in laryngotracheal stenosis: a systematic review and meta-analysis.

treatment_algorithms.title: Therapeutic algorithm for attempting endoscopic interventions (Monnier et al.)
specific_recommendations: Attempt endoscopic interventions first when SGS is grade I/II, stenosis <1.5 cm craniocaudal, membranous type, with adequate cartilaginous support.
decision_points_and_pathways: If SGS grade I/II AND stenosis <1.5 cm AND membranous type AND adequate cartilage, then attempt endoscopic intervention first.
treatment_algorithms.patient_population_criteria: SGS meeting grade I/II, <1.5 cm, membranous, adequate cartilaginous support.
alternative_approaches: Reserve surgery for selected cases and relapsing stenoses (as per cited experience).
treatment_algorithms.source_excerpt: stating that endoscopic interventions should be attempted first in the presence of SGS grade I/II, stenosis <1.5 cm in a craniocaudal direction, and membranous type with an adequate cartilaginous support.

clinical_guidelines.title: Endoscopic treatment for simple subglottic stenoses and multidisciplinary management for complex cases
specific_recommendations: Endoscopic treatment has a high success rate for simple stenoses.
Endoscopic treatment is a valid option for patients who are unsuitable candidates for surgery.
Complex stenoses often require a multidisciplinary approach.
decision_points_and_pathways: Simple stenosis -> consider endoscopic treatment.
Unsuitable surgical candidate -> consider endoscopic treatment.
Complex stenosis -> multidisciplinary approach.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Endoscopic treatment has a high success rate for simple stenoses and is a valid option for patients who are unsuitable candidates for surgery. Complex stenoses often require a multidisciplinary approach.

clinical_guidelines.title: Prevention of traumatic subglottic stenosis
specific_recommendations: High tracheotomy and cricothyroidotomy are only performed in extreme emergencies.
Avoid aggressive endoscopic manipulation for benign laryngeal lesions.
Perform intubation and endoscopy gently.
Recognize and prevent factors contributing to laryngeal trauma after intubation when possible.
decision_points_and_pathways: Extreme emergencies -> high tracheotomy or cricothyroidotomy may be performed; otherwise avoid.
outcome_measures: Incidence of traumatic SGS can be radically reduced.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: The incidence of traumatic SGS can be radically reduced if high tracheotomy and cricothyroidotomy are only performed in extreme emergencies; aggressive endoscopic manipulation for benign laryngeal lesions is avoided; intubation

clinical_guidelines.title: Management of subglottic stenosis in granulomatosis with polyangiitis
clinical_guidelines.condition: Subglottic stenosis in granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA)
specific_recommendations: Systemic immunosuppressive therapy is the mainstay of treatment in GPA.

Endoscopic management of subglottic lesions (laser resection, serial dilations, topical corticosteroids, local mitomycin-c) is an important aspect in those who remain symptomatic, despite appropriate medical management.
decision_points_and_pathways: Symptomatic despite appropriate medical management -> endoscopic management of subglottic lesions (laser resection, serial dilations, topical corticosteroids, local mitomycin-c).
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Those who remain symptomatic, despite appropriate medical management.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Systemic immunosuppressive therapy is the mainstay of treatment in GPA.

clinical_guidelines.title: Stage-based treatment for laryngeal scleroma with subglottic involvement
clinical_guidelines.condition: Subglottic stenosis secondary to laryngeal scleroma
specific_recommendations: Treatment should be based on the clinical stage, severity, and anatomical location.
In the proliferative phase, long-term antibiotics are the treatment of choice.
In the fibrotic stage, if the patient is symptomatic and there is mild subglottic involvement, endoscopic procedures can be valid therapeutic options.
Open surgical techniques have been attempted for extensive SGS.
decision_points_and_pathways: Proliferative phase -> long-term antibiotics.
Fibrotic stage + symptomatic + mild subglottic involvement -> endoscopic procedures.
Extensive SGS -> open surgical techniques have been attempted.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Symptomatic patients with mild subglottic involvement in the fibrotic stage.
alternative_approaches: Open surgical techniques have been attempted for extensive SGS.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Treatment should be based on the clinical stage, severity, and anatomical location. In the proliferative phase, long-term antibiotics are the treatment of choice. In the fibrotic stage

clinical_guidelines.title: Management of laryngotracheal amyloidosis with subglottic obstruction
clinical_guidelines.condition: Subglottic obstructive lesions due to amyloidosis
specific_recommendations: Bronchoscopy-based techniques (laser therapy, stenting) have been suggested as a possible method for treating subglottic obstructive lesions.
Excision, when possible, remains the treatment of choice in localized forms of amyloidosis.
decision_points_and_pathways: Localized forms of amyloidosis -> excision remains the treatment of choice.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Bronchoscopy-based techniques (laser therapy, stenting) have been suggested as a possible method for treating subglottic obstructive lesions. Excision, when possible, remains the treatment of choice

clinical_guidelines.title: Airway management in relapsing polychondritis
specific_recommendations: Diagnose and plan treatment promptly before irreversible damage occurs.
Medical management of RP focuses on suppressing the acute inflammatory process.
It is possible to treat these patients by endoscopic procedures (e.g., dilation, stenting).
Occasionally, involvement of the glottis and subglottic regions may require tracheotomy.
decision_points_and_pathways: Airway disease with persistent issues -> endoscopic procedures (e.g., dilation, stenting).
Glottic and subglottic region involvement -> may require tracheotomy.
outcome_measures: The majority experience improvement in respiratory symptoms.
alternative_approaches: Tracheotomy may be required for glottic and subglottic involvement.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Medical management of RP focuses on suppressing the acute inflammatory process. Ernst and colleagues have shown that it is possible to treat these patients by endoscopic procedures

clinical_guidelines.title: Management of recurrent respiratory papillomatosis with airway involvement
clinical_guidelines.condition: Recurrent papillomatosis involving the larynx, trachea, or bronchi
specific_recommendations: Endoscopic interventions are crucial, as repeated treatment is usually necessary due to recurrence.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Endoscopic interventions are crucial, as repeated treatment is usually necessary due to recurrence.

clinical_guidelines.title: Treatment considerations for congenital subglottic stenosis types
specific_recommendations: The cartilaginous type is rarely successfully treated with endoscopic techniques.
decision_points_and_pathways: Cartilaginous type vs membranous type -> endoscopic success is rare in cartilaginous type.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: It is often more severe than the membranous type and is rarely successfully treated with endoscopic techniques.

clinical_guidelines.title: Flexible bronchoscopy as gold standard for pre-interventional assessment
specific_recommendations: Use flexible bronchoscopy as the gold standard for evaluation prior to any interventional attempts.
Assess supraglottic/glottic and subglottic abnormalities, stenosis length/severity, vocal cord mobility, distance from cords, dynamic airway, cartilage involvement, and scar maturity.
Examine the tracheobronchial tree for secondary lesions and the suprastomal area if tracheotomy present or planned.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients with suspected SGS undergoing pre-interventional assessment.
alternative_approaches: Can be performed awake under local anesthesia, or under mild/moderate sedation or general anesthesia depending on goals.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Flexible bronchoscopy is the gold standard for the evaluation of these patients as it is an effective method of obtaining preliminary information prior to any interventional attempts.

clinical_guidelines.title: Rigid bronchoscopy for accurate measurement; avoid traumatic ETT sizing
specific_recommendations: Use rigid bronchoscopy under general anesthesia to accurately measure stenosis length and diameter and plan treatment.
Avoid assessing stenosis by inserting progressively larger endotracheal tubes due to risk of iatrogenic injury.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients with SGS requiring accurate airway measurements for planning.
contraindications_and_exceptions: Caution: progressive ETT upsizing may cause further injury.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Caution should be taken with this method as it may cause further iatrogenic injury to the airway.

clinical_guidelines.title: Radiologic evaluation with high-resolution CT/MRI; use dynamic expiratory CT when indicated
specific_recommendations: Prefer high-resolution CT and MRI over standard radiographs for detailed airway and adjacent structure assessment.
Use dynamic expiratory CT to detect excessive airway collapse associated with SGS.
Use MRI to assess vascular compression or mediastinal tumor extent when indicated.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients with SGS undergoing imaging evaluation.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Dynamic expiratory CT also helps to detect excessive airway collapse, which may be associated with SGS.

clinical_guidelines.title: Include functional, serological, reflux exams; spirometry threshold for extrathoracic obstruction
specific_recommendations: Include functional (lung function, swallowing), serological (ANCA-c, ACE), and reflux exams (24 hour esophageal pH-impedance, esophagoscopy).
Use spirometry to assess level and degree of obstruction.
Use FEV1/PEF >0.50 to discriminate extrathoracic airway obstruction from asthma or COPD, supporting SGS diagnosis.
decision_points_and_pathways: If FEV1/PEF >0.50, supports extrathoracic airway obstruction rather than asthma/COPD.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients evaluated for SGS.
monitoring_requirements: Use flow-volume loops and spirometric values to compare post-intervention with pre-intervention for therapeutic efficacy.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: The ratio of forced expiratory volume in 1s (FEV1) to the peak expiratory flow (PEF) >0.50 can discriminate between extrathoracic airway obstruction and asthma or COPD

clinical_guidelines.title: Conservative management for minimally symptomatic or mild SGS
specific_recommendations: For minimally symptomatic, stable, non-progressive adult SGS without quality-of-life impact: close monitoring may suffice.
For a child with mild stenosis: conservative treatment with regular follow-up and anticipation of growth may obviate further therapy.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Adults with stable, minimally symptomatic SGS; children with mild stenosis.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: A minimally symptomatic adult patient with stable non-progressive SGS, with no impact on quality of life, can be successfully managed with close monitoring.

clinical_guidelines.title: Endoscopic modalities: indications and use cases
specific_recommendations: Use endoscopic modalities as first option for short segment, membranous, benign, concentric SGS not involving cartilage.
Use to maintain a safe airway while waiting for other treatments.

Use for treatment/palliation in patients not surgical candidates due to stenosis characteristics, active local infection, severe inflammation, poor general medical status, or unstable coexisting diseases.
Use to treat restenosis following open reconstructive procedures.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Short segment membranous benign concentric SGS; patients awaiting other treatment; non-surgical candidates; restenosis after open surgery.
alternative_approaches: Open surgical management when endoscopic criteria are not met or after multiple recurrences.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Endoscopic modalities may be the first option for short segment, membranous, benign, concentric SGS not involving the cartilage; for maintaining a safe airway while waiting for other treatments

clinical_guidelines.title: Avoid argon plasma coagulation; prioritize epithelial preservation and laser techniques
specific_recommendations: Preserve airway epithelium with minimal trauma for good outcomes.
Do not use argon plasma coagulation for SGS due to uncontrolled tissue destruction risk.
Use laser (CO2 or Nd:YAG) for precise scar vaporization, minimizing bleeding and edema.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients selected for endoscopic resection of SGS.
contraindications_and_exceptions: Argon plasma coagulation is not an option for SGS.
alternative_approaches: Electrocautery knife in cutting mode when appropriate.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: argon plasma coagulation is not an option for SGS as it can cause uncontrolled tissue destruction.

clinical_guidelines.title: Radial incisions plus gentle dilation for short, web-like stenoses
specific_recommendations: Create mucosal trapdoor flaps or radial incisions in 3–4 quadrants to release the constricting ring while preserving intact mucosa.
Combine with gentle dilation to improve long-term results, with reported success in selected cases.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Selected short, web-like stenoses.
outcome_measures: Long-term success (reported 75% in selected short, web-like stenoses).
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: this cutting method with gentle dilation may produce better long-term results [22], with a 75% success rate in selected cases (short, web-like stenoses).

clinical_guidelines.title: Factors associated with high endoscopic failure
specific_recommendations: Recognize risk factors for failure: circumferential scarring, interarytenoid posterior commissure fibrosis, severe tracheal infection, perichondrium/cartilage exposure during laser excision, combined laryngotracheal stenosis, prior failed endoscopic repair, vertical scar length >1 cm, significant loss of cartilaginous support.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients considered for endoscopic management of SGS.
contraindications_and_exceptions: Vertical scar length >1 cm and significant cartilage loss are associated with high endoscopic failure.
alternative_approaches: Consider open surgical approaches when high-risk features are present.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: vertical scar length >1 cm; and significant loss of cartilaginous support [21, 22].

clinical_guidelines.title: Use of dilation techniques: balloon dilation and combinations
specific_recommendations: Balloon dilators provide gentle dilation without shearing mucosa; effective for soft, short, isolated SGS in adults and pediatric patients.
In extensive or firm SGS, dilation alone is relatively ineffective; combine with other procedures to increase success.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Soft, short, isolated SGS; more extensive/firm SGS when combined with other modalities.
alternative_approaches: Combine with resection, adjuvant therapy, or stenting when indicated.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: This method has been shown to be effective in the management of soft, short and isolated SGS, in adult and pediatric patients

clinical_guidelines.title: Mitomycin-C topical application parameters and safety precautions
specific_recommendations: Apply mitomycin-C at 0.4 mg/ml topically to subglottic scar excision.
Use 2–3 applications of 2 min each or a single application of 4–5 min, with subsequent saline irrigation.
Avoid higher concentrations; serious complications may occur.
Avoid contact with unprotected skin or eyes; follow proper disposal protocols.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients undergoing laser and/or dilation where adjuvant antiproliferative therapy is planned.
contraindications_and_exceptions: Higher concentrations should be avoided due to risk of serious complications.
alternative_approaches: Other adjuvants include topical corticosteroids, halofuginone, colchicine, tamoxifen, 5-fluorouracil.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: at a concentration of 0.4 mg/ml and applied topically to the area of subglottic scar excision (2–3 applications of 2 min each or single application of 4–5 min).

clinical_guidelines.title: Airway stenting: indications and contraindications
specific_recommendations: Consider stenting after failure of resection and/or for benign complex stenosis in non-surgical candidates.

Indications include inflammatory/infectious stenosis while awaiting systemic therapy or open surgery, restenosis after open surgery, extrinsic compression, expiratory collapse, and patient preference.
Any endoluminal or intrinsic airway pathology with >50% lumen reduction after other treatments may indicate stenting.
Contraindications: active stenoses following burns or blast injuries; severe dysphagia.
decision_points_and_pathways: If >50% lumen reduction persists after other treatments, consider stenting.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: SGS patients meeting indication scenarios above.
contraindications_and_exceptions: Active stenoses following burns or blast injuries.
alternative_approaches: Montgomery T-tube via tracheotomy to avoid migration in selected patients.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Any endoluminal or intrinsic airway pathology that causes more than 50% lumen reduction after other treatments may be an indication for stenting.

clinical_guidelines.title: Stent positioning safety margin from vocal cords
clinical_guidelines.condition: Subglottic stenosis (SGS) requiring stenting near glottis
specific_recommendations: Maintain approximately 10 mm distance from the vocal cords to the proximal end of the stent whenever possible to reduce granulation risk.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients receiving subglottic stents where proximity to vocal cords is a concern.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: A distance of 10 mm from the vocal cords to the proximal end of the stent seems to be an acceptable safety margin, whenever possible

clinical_guidelines.title: Bronchoscopic surveillance after stent placement
specific_recommendations: Perform bronchoscopic surveillance to detect and treat stent complications and to monitor efficacy.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients with benign airway stents for SGS.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Bronchoscopic surveillance is advisable to detect and treat stent complications and to monitor efficacy

clinical_guidelines.title: Avoid expandable metallic stents in benign SGS; reserve for malignant palliation
specific_recommendations: Do not use expandable metallic stents for benign SGS due to significant long-term complications.
Reserve metallic stents for palliation in malignant SGS etiologies.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients being considered for airway stenting in SGS.
contraindications_and_exceptions: Benign SGS is a contraindication for permanent expandable metallic stents.
alternative_approaches: Consider silicone stents; customized 3D or biodegradable stents are options but require improvements.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Expandable metallic stents should be avoided due to the significant long-term complications that are associated with the placement of permanent stents in benign conditions and should be reserved for palliation in malignant SGS etiologies.

clinical_guidelines.title: European Laryngological Society recommendation: primary open surgery for mature high-grade adult SGS
clinical_guidelines.condition: Subglottic stenosis (SGS), mature high-grade in adults
specific_recommendations: Treat mature high-grade SGS in adults primarily by open surgery, as chances of success are generally best at the first procedure.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Adults with mature high-grade SGS.
alternative_approaches: Endoscopic management may be used in selected cases; open surgery plays a key role especially in complex stenosis or multiple recurrences.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: The European Laryngological Society recommends that mature high-grade stenosis in adults should be treated primarily by open surgery, as the chances of success are generally best at the first procedure

clinical_guidelines.title: Surgical caution in GPA and persistent inflammation
clinical_guidelines.condition: Subglottic stenosis (SGS) in systemic diseases (e.g., GPA)
specific_recommendations: Perform invasive procedures with extreme caution in GPA due to risk of aggravating vasculitis and causing restenosis.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients with SGS and systemic diseases with persistent inflammation (e.g., GPA).
contraindications_and_exceptions: Certain surgical modalities may aggravate vasculitis and increase restenosis risk.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: In systemic diseases with persistent inflammation, such as GPA, invasive procedures should be performed with extreme caution

clinical_guidelines.title: Post-endoscopic follow-up and adjunct medical therapy
specific_recommendations: Close follow-up and monitoring are essential.
Post-endoscopic approaches may include systemic antibiotics, systemic corticosteroids, and active anti-gastroesophageal reflux management (not proven in randomized trials).
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients after endoscopic interventions for SGS.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Close follow-up and monitoring are essential.

clinical_guidelines.title: Multidisciplinary management approach
specific_recommendations: Use a multidisciplinary approach involving interventional pulmonologists, otolaryngologists, thoracic surgeons, gastroenterologists, and speech language pathologists.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients with SGS requiring comprehensive care planning.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: A multidisciplinary approach involving interventional pulmonologists, otolaryngologists, thoracic surgeons, gastroenterologists, and speech language pathologists is used in many centers.

clinical_guidelines.title: Immediate postoperative reassessment and bronchoscopy planning in SGS
specific_recommendations: Wound reassessment is performed regularly in the first few weeks after surgery (<2–4 weeks) to determine the status of airway healing, stent position and patency
Appropriate tracheotomy care is of paramount importance
In these circumstances, bronchoscopy is important to assess airway patency and plan decannulation
decision_points_and_pathways: First few weeks after surgery (<2–4 weeks): perform wound reassessment to determine airway healing, stent position/patency
Use bronchoscopy to assess airway patency and plan decannulation
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Post-surgery SGS patients
clinical_guidelines.monitoring_requirements: Regular reassessment in the first few weeks after surgery (<2–4 weeks); bronchoscopy as needed to assess patency and plan decannulation
clinical_guidelines.outcome_measures: Status of airway healing; stent position and patency; readiness for decannulation
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Wound reassessment is performed regularly in the first few weeks after surgery (<2–4 weeks) to determine the status of airway healing, stent position and patency,

clinical_guidelines.title: Long-term bronchoscopy follow-up after SGS intervention
specific_recommendations: For the first 1–2 years post-intervention, intermittent bronchoscopy is recommended
In other patients, the duration of follow-up depends on the duration of stent placement and symptoms after stent removal
Bronchoscopy should be considered whenever the patient presents with symptoms of airway obstruction
decision_points_and_pathways: First 1–2 years post-intervention: perform intermittent bronchoscopy to allow long-term evaluation and detection of recurrent stenosis before it reaches a critical stage
Adjust follow-up based on duration of stent placement and symptoms after stent removal
Consider bronchoscopy whenever airway obstruction symptoms are present
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Post-intervention SGS patients (including those with prior stent placement or removal)
clinical_guidelines.monitoring_requirements: Intermittent bronchoscopy during the first 1–2 years post-intervention; symptom-triggered bronchoscopy thereafter
clinical_guidelines.outcome_measures: Long-term evaluation and detection of recurrent stenosis before critical stage
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: For the first 1–2 years post-intervention, intermittent bronchoscopy is recommended because it allows long-term evaluation and detection of recurrent stenosis before it reaches a critical stage.

clinical_guidelines.title: Treatment approach selection for SGS based on stenosis complexity
specific_recommendations: Endoscopic procedures can be used to treat different types and grades of SGS
Scientific evidence suggests that they are the first choice for simple stenoses
Complex stenoses often need a multidisciplinary approach and may require surgery
Major and repeated procedures themselves, if not thoughtfully planned as part of a management strategy, can cause additional injury and significant morbidity
decision_points_and_pathways: If stenosis is simple: choose endoscopic procedures as first choice
If stenosis is complex: use a multidisciplinary approach and consider surgery
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: SGS patients with simple versus complex stenosis
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: Avoid major and repeated procedures if not thoughtfully planned due to risk of additional injury and significant morbidity
clinical_guidelines.outcome_measures: Treatment of SGS can improve dyspnea and patient-reported quality of life
clinical_guidelines.alternative_approaches: Surgery for complex stenoses when indicated
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Scientific evidence suggests that they are the first choice for simple stenoses, whereas complex stenoses often need a multidisciplinary approach and may require surgery.

clinical_guidelines.title: European Laryngological Society (ELS) distinction: fresh incipient vs mature cicatricial SGS
clinical_guidelines.condition: Classify SGS stage of wound healing
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: the European Laryngological Society distinguishes between fresh incipient SGS (resulting from acute or subacute post-intubation airway narrowing with edema, ulceration, granulation tissue) and mature cicatricial SGS

Abstract
Subglottic stenosis (SGS) is a challenging therapeutic
problem for the interventional pulmonologist

Depending
on the etiology it can be classiﬁed as congenital or
acquired

Acquired causes are often due to iatrogenic
injury but can also result from tumors, infections, and
rare diseases such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis,
relapsing polychondritis, and amyloidosis
